executiveSummary:
Momentum is strong with ARR growth well above benchmarks, improving profitability, and efficient customer acquisition; however, durability is the constraint. Retention metrics are below SaaS norms and growth is skewed to new logos over expansion, while G&A is persistently over budget despite overall cost efficiency gains. The priority is to convert healthy new logo momentum into durable, efficient, profitable growth.

  • Retention and expansion quality: Gross retention (79%), logo retention (85%), and NRR (90%) lag while ARR is driven primarily by new land. The data indicates focus on diagnosing churn/downgrade patterns and lifting expansion via packaging/pricing and success motions commonly used to raise NRR.
  • Cost discipline with emphasis on G&A: EBIT has improved to positive and efficiency metrics are strong (CAC ratio ~0.5; LTV:CAC ~6.5), but G&A is materially over budget. Typical actions include spend reviews, pacing controls, and benchmark-based right-sizing as operating leverage increases.
  • Scaling the new logo engine sustainably: Recent growth is concentrated in specific verticals (Energy & Utilities) and regions (Americas), with expansions under budget. Consider pipeline quality analysis by segment, win-rate/pricing reviews, and onboarding-to-value tracking to protect payback and future expansion.
page1:
Overall health shows high growth with improving profitability and strong efficiency: ARR £9.4m with 70% growth; Rule of 40 at 63%; CAC ratio 0.56 and LTV:CAC 6.5. EBIT remains slightly negative on the dashboard (-7%) but improving across the P&L trend. The constraint is durability: gross retention at 79%, logo retention 85%, and NRR 90% are below typical benchmarks despite a high recurring revenue mix (94%). Cost mix continues to shift favorably with S&M 37%, development 28%, and general 20%.

  • Management focus reinforcement: The retention and expansion gap evidenced here supports the pack-wide emphasis on diagnosing churn drivers and improving expansion mechanics, while sustaining cost discipline as efficiency is strong.
page2:
Growth is consistently driven by new logos and land ARR additions. Total logos rise from 68 (Mar-25) to 168 (Dec-27), and ARR scales from £6.8m to £17.6m. Net ARR additions are robust across periods, but retention is volatile: logo retention dips to 81% at times and net retention is sub-100% in several periods (e.g., Dec-25 91%, Mar-27 96%, Sep-27 93%), indicating expansion is not fully offsetting churn and downsell.

This pattern is consistent with a land-led engine that has not yet translated into sustained expansion at scale.

  • Management focus reinforcement: Prioritize retention analytics (lost logo/downsizing reasons by cohort and deal size) and review of expansion levers (usage thresholds, seat/feature packaging) to push NRR toward or above 100%.
page3:
Margins and operating leverage are improving. Gross margin remains ~78–79% while operating costs as a percentage of revenue trend down (S&M from 45% to 24%). EBIT improves from -21% to +8% by Dec-27. Efficiency ratios remain strong (CAC ~0.51; LTV:CAC ~15 by Dec-27). Headcount scales from 53 to 106, with the largest absolute increase in Development, supporting product velocity but requiring continued cost governance.

Budget variance patterns highlight G&A pressure elsewhere in the pack; mixing effects and scaling suggest careful oversight is warranted as the organization grows.

  • Management focus reinforcement: Tighten G&A controls via line-by-line spend reviews and pacing relative to revenue, a common SaaS practice as profitability inflects, while maintaining discipline on hiring mix to preserve ARR per head.
page4:
ARR composition shows concentration and durability considerations. Vertically, Energy & Utilities accounts for c.41% of ARR (c.£4.0m), with Life Science ~26%; regionally, revenue is diversified but Americas are largest in aggregate. The 12‑month waterfall is land-led (Land £4.32m; Expand £0.71m; Downsells -£0.27m; Lost -£0.88m), and the rolling NRR stepped down from 108% to ~90–92% by period end, indicating expansion isn’t consistently offsetting churn and downgrades.

The mix implies sensitivity to retention/expansion execution within key verticals and regions despite healthy new demand.

  • Management focus reinforcement: Deep-dive retention/expansion by vertical and region (e.g., Energy & Utilities vs. Government; Americas vs. Europe) to identify packaging, adoption, and service patterns that typically unlock higher NRR.
page5:
Recent movements are positive and new-logo led: last three months delivered £855k ARR, driven by £720k from new logos across eight wins and £180k in expansion; downsell was limited (-£45k). Energy & Utilities and Government contributed most of the recent new ARR, with activity concentrated in South and North America and Africa.

Early signals suggest the land engine remains healthy, but expansion remains a smaller share of growth in the near term.

  • Management focus reinforcement: Assess onboarding quality-to-expansion conversion for the newest cohorts in the contributing segments, a common lever to accelerate time-to-first expansion and lift NRR.
page6:
Performance versus budget is slightly ahead on the top line and ARR, with mixed quality underneath. Annual revenue is +1% versus budget and EBITDA is modestly better (+£30k). ARR is +11% versus budget, driven by higher additions (+£329k) and better-than-budget attrition, partially offset by weaker upsell and slightly higher downsell. Cost variances show S&M and Development favorable to budget, but G&A is materially over budget (-38%) at annual, quarterly, and monthly levels.

The data indicates solid commercial execution with cost discipline in go-to-market and product, but emphasizes the need to rein in G&A to preserve operating leverage as scale increases.

  • Management focus reinforcement: Implement G&A variance analysis and benchmarks-based targets (e.g., G&A % of revenue) with monthly pacing controls, while exploring upsell drivers to close the gap to budgeted expansion.
